Background chicken meat extract is a popular functional food in Asia. It is rich in the bioactive compounds carnosine and anserine, two histidine-containing dipeptides (HCD). Studies suggest that acute pre-exercise ingestion of chicken extracts has important applications towards exercise performance and fatigue control, but the evidence is equivocal. This study aimed to evaluate the ergogenic potential of the pre-exercise ingestion of a homemade chicken broth (CB) vs a placebo soup on a short-lasting, high-intensity cycling exercise. Methods fourteen men participated in this double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover intervention study. Subjects ingested either CB, thereby receiving 46.4 mg/kg body weight of HCD, or a placebo soup (similar in taste without HCD) 40 min before an 8 min cycling time trial (TT) was performed. Venous blood samples were collected at arrival (fasted), before exercise and at 5 min recovery. Plasma HCD were measured with UPLC-MS/MS and glutathione (in red blood cells) was measured through HPLC. Capillary blood samples were collected at different timepoints before and after exercise. Results a significant improvement ( p = 0.033; 5.2%) of the 8 min TT mean power was observed after CB supplementation compared to placebo. Post-exercise plasma carnosine ( p < 0.05) and anserine ( p < 0.001) was significantly increased after CB supplementation and not following placebo. No significant effect of CB supplementation was observed either on blood glutathione levels, nor on capillary blood analysis. Conclusions oral CB supplementation improved the 8 min TT performance albeit it did not affect the acid-base balance or oxidative status parameters. Further research should unravel the potential role and mechanisms of HCD, present in CB, in this ergogenic approach. Keywords Carnosine Anserine Chicken broth Pre-exercise meal High-intensity exercise Performance Industrial Research Fund (IOF, Ghent University) F2014/IOF-StarTT/273 Derave Wim issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2021 Background Chicken meat and its extracts have long been recognized as a source of bioactive molecules that can potentially improve health status in general, and exercise performance in particular. In traditional South-Asian medicine, chicken extracts are used to alleviate stress or mild disease symptoms [ 1 ]. The activities of chicken extracts are suggested to be related to its active components, including proteins, free amino acids, taurine, many minerals, trace elements, and vitamins. In addition, chicken meat extracts contain high concentrations of carnosine (β-alanyl-L-histidine) and anserine (β-alanyl-π-methyl-histidine) in a 1:2 to 1:3 ratio [ 2 , 3 ]. Carnosine and its methylated analogue anserine are histidine-containing dipeptides (HCD) present in high concentrations in skeletal muscle of mammals and therefore abundantly present in the daily food of non-vegetarian persons [ 2 ]. Harris et al. [ 4 ] demonstrated that long-term administration of β-alanine - one of the constituent amino acids - is able to raise muscle carnosine concentrations, which leads to enhanced high-intensity exercise performance [ 5 , 6 ]. The chronic use of chicken breast extract, containing carnosine and anserine, is shown to enhance muscle carnosine levels in humans [ 7 ] and to improve high-intensity endurance performance by attenuation of muscle fatigue [ 8 ], demonstrating the same mechanism of action of the β-alanine supplementation approach. In contrast to chronic supplementation strategies, aiming to promote muscle carnosine loading (thus increasing the intracellular muscle pH-buffer capacity), it can be hypothesized that acute supplementation, leading to elevated circulating HCD, may exert ergogenic effects through attenuation of acidosis and/or oxidative stress in blood. Unfortunately, the bioavailability of carnosine in the circulation following supplementation is very low in humans due to the fast breakdown by the very active human serum carnosinase-1 (CN1) enzyme, and acute carnosine supplementation (20 mg/kg BW) could not elicit improvements in a high-intensity cycling test [ 9 ]. Interestingly, both in vitro [ 3 , 10 , 11 ] and in vivo [ 12 , 13 ] experiments revealed that anserine is much less prone to hydrolysis by carnosinase due to the lower affinity to the CN1 enzyme, suggesting that anserine or a combination of anserine plus carnosine might be required to induce acute ergogenic effects. A recent study of Blancquaert et al. (unpublished, congress presentation: http://hdl.handle.net/1854/LU-8642579 ) demonstrated increased HCD stability in the circulation by a combination of pure (chemically synthesized) carnosine and anserine ingestion in a 1:1 ratio (25 mg/kg BW of each) compared to anserine alone (25 mg/kg BW). In addition, performance-enhancing effects of this pre-exercise supplementation strategy were found on maximal Wingate power in healthy humans. The ergogenic potential of acute pre-exercise supplementation of chicken extracts (containing both carnosine and anserine) is already tested by Suzuki and colleagues, but the results are so far inconclusive. Suzuki et al. [ 14 ] showed that the pre-exercise intake of the chicken breast extract (denominated as CBEX™), containing 0.4 g carnosine and 1.1 g anserine, enhanced the power output of the latter half of 2 sets of repeated sprints. In a follow-up study using the same supplementation strategy for a single set of similar repeated sprints, no improvement on performance was found, although a positive effect on exercise-induced acid-base balance was present [ 15 ]. Informed by this emerging evidence for an acute effect of pre-exercise supplementation of pure HCD on exercise performance, we evaluated the effect of a similar dose of HCD in a functional food approach, i.e. through a home-prepared chicken broth (CB) vs a placebo soup (PLA), in a cross-over nutritional intervention study. The purpose of this study is to examine the ergogenic effect of the chicken broth (CB), according to the recipe from Harris et al. [ 4 ], administered as a 40-min pre-exercise snack, on a short-lasting, high-intensity cycling exercise (8 min cycling time-trial). The type and duration of the exercise were aimed to challenge the possible ergogenic effects of anserine and carnosine in the CB based on their contribution to the intracellular acid-base balance as well as oxidative stress control [ 16 , 17 ].

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Acute pre-exercise chicken broth (CB) ingestion, a nutritional intervention containing high concentrations of histidine-containing dipeptides (HCDs), utilized for performance enhancement during short-term, high-intensity cycling exercise (e.g., an 8-min time trial).
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Acute pre-exercise ingestion of chicken broth (CB), rich in histidine-containing dipeptides (HCDs) like carnosine and anserine, is hypothesized to exert ergogenic effects primarily through mechanisms other than direct attenuation of acidosis or oxidative stress in the blood, as no significant changes were observed in parameters like pH, lactate, bicarbonate, or glutathione levels. While chronic HCD supplementation can increase muscle carnosine and pH-buffering capacity, the acute effect observed here is linked to elevated circulating HCDs, particularly anserine, which accumulates to a much greater extent than carnosine due to its lower susceptibility to hydrolysis by human serum carnosinase-1 (CN1). The exact underlying ergogenic mechanism for the observed performance improvement, which extends beyond pH buffering and antioxidant capacity, remains unclear and warrants further research, potentially leading to therapeutic applications.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Participants acutely ingested chicken broth (CB) at a dose of 8 mL/kg body weight, providing 46.4 mg/kg body weight of total histidine-containing dipeptides (HCDs), specifically 15.6 mg/kg BW carnosine and 30.8 mg/kg BW anserine. This dose, equivalent to about 350g of chicken breast, was notably higher (twice) than doses used in some previous studies by Suzuki et al. This specific CB supplementation significantly improved mean power output and increased plasma carnosine and anserine levels compared to a placebo. In contrast, prior acute supplementation with 20 mg/kg BW pure carnosine alone did not yield performance improvements, though combined ingestion of 25 mg/kg BW each of pure carnosine and anserine showed increased HCD stability and performance benefits.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The specificity of the chicken broth (CB) intervention was confirmed by comparing it against a HCD-free placebo soup, with careful dietary controls (vegetarian meal pre-test) and sensitive plasma HCD analysis to prevent bias. While CB supplementation significantly improved performance and elevated plasma carnosine and anserine, these effects appear specifically linked to the HCD content, with anserine accumulating approximately 50 times more than carnosine due to its lower susceptibility to hydrolysis by human serum carnosinase-1 (CN1). Despite the performance improvement, CB did not significantly impact blood glutathione levels, acid-base balance (pH, lactate, bicarbonate), or other capillary blood parameters (glucose, Ca2+, Cl-, Na+, K+), suggesting a mechanism independent of these. Although HCDs are considered pivotal, the study could not entirely exclude the involvement of other macro- and micronutrients in the broth. The full spectrum of performance benefits from CB supplementation remains to be further defined.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: The study population consisted of 14 healthy, moderately to recreationally-trained men (13 completed analysis), with an average age of 37.2  1 6.5 years, weight of 76.2  1 10.0 kg, and relative maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) of 50.0  1 5.5 mL/min/kg. Inclusion criteria specified males, non-vegetarian status, no drug or food supplement intake for 3 months prior to or during the study, and engagement in medium-high weekly training habits (approximately 10 hours/week). The findings require further extrapolation to well-trained athletes and women, as they were not included in this study.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Acute pre-exercise ingestion of chicken broth (CB) significantly improves performance during short-lasting, high-intensity cycling exercise, specifically demonstrating a sizeable 5.2% improvement in an 8-minute cycling time-trial. This represents a novel dietary approach and an ergogenic benefit for sports, aiding in the optimization of performance for individuals undertaking such intense physical activities.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Protective benefit. No adverse symptoms or side-effects were reported following chicken broth ingestion in this study. It is noted that while high doses of pure carnosine (60 mg/kg BW) can induce side effects such as headache and paraesthesia, the combined ingestion of carnosine and anserine within a food matrix, as in chicken broth, appears to mitigate these risks.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The study demonstrated a reliable and significant ergogenic effect of homemade chicken broth on performance and markedly increased plasma concentrations of carnosine and anserine. The quantification of these dipeptides in both the broth and plasma utilized highly reliable methods, including HPLC-fluorescence and an in-house developed and validated UPLC-MS/MS method. This UPLC-MS/MS method demonstrated excellent linearity (r > 0.99), precision, and sensitivity (LODs of 5.72 nmol/L for carnosine and 10.61 nmol/L for anserine), adhering to international guidelines. While carnosine's bioavailability is generally low due to rapid degradation by serum carnosinase-1 (CN1), anserine shows greater stability. Despite previous equivocal evidence for acute chicken extract effects, this study provides strong evidence for the efficacy of CB. However, the extent to which these findings can be extrapolated to well-trained athletes and women needs further investigation.
recommended_alternatives: Combination of anserine plus carnosine (for acute ergogenic effects)
Further research on the potential role and mechanisms of HCD in chicken broth
Further investigation into the specific underlying ergogenic mechanism beyond pH buffering and antioxidant properties.
Comparison of findings from pure HCD supplement powders versus functional food approaches to confirm shared mechanisms.
Investigation into the involvement of other macro- and micronutrients in chicken broth
Studies to extrapolate findings to well-trained athletes and women.
